q: Why does this course teach you to read disassembly, though you never write assembly?
choices: Some bugs can only be explained by the instructions the compiler emitted
Assembly is required for every interrupt handler
C cannot reach peripheral registers without it
The exam asks you to write short assembly routines for each peripheral driver
why: When the debugger stops with no source line, a variable changes by itself or the optimiser deletes code, the answer is in what the compiler actually emitted. Reading it is a diagnostic skill.

q: Which instruction set does every Cortex-M execute?
why: Every Cortex-M executes Thumb only. Cortex-A and Cortex-R hold both and switch between them.

q: Under what circumstances does a Cortex-M switch into ARM (A32) state?
choices: Never: it has no ARM state
When a branch target has bit 0 clear
When code runs in Handler mode
why: There is no ARM state to switch to. Branching to an even address tells the core to run ARM code, and it faults rather than switches.

q: Roughly how much smaller is the same program in Thumb than in ARM (A32)?
why: Thumb is about 30% smaller: 16-bit instructions widened to 32 bits only when they must be.

q: What is the main reason Thumb exists?
choices: Code density: more program per byte of memory
Access to more registers per instruction
why: A compressed instruction set is about code density, because memory is what a small system runs out of first. Thumb actually reaches fewer registers (R0–R7) in most forms.

q: Thumb is ARM's compressed instruction set. Which is RISC-V's equivalent?
why: RISC-V's compressed encoding is the C extension; MIPS's was MIPS16. AArch64 is ARM's 64-bit instruction set, not a compressed one.

q: About how many distinct mnemonics make up 80% of real firmware on this chip?
why: Thirteen mnemonics (movs, ldr, cmp, str, adds, bl, lsls, b, bne, beq, subs, push, pop) make up about 80% of the spike's code.

q: Why is lsls more common than subs in embedded code?
choices: Bit fields: every (value << (pin*2)) compiles to a shift
Shifts are the only way to multiply on the M0+
The compiler uses lsls to clear flags
lsls is needed to load addresses from the literal pool
why: Peripheral configuration is shift-and-mask, so a shift outranks subtraction. The M0+ does have muls.

q: What defines a load–store architecture?
choices: Only load and store instructions touch memory; the ALU sees registers only
Every instruction may take a memory operand
Loads and stores are combined with the arithmetic into one long instruction
Data must be loaded into a cache before use
why: Load–store: ALU operands are registers only and memory is reached only by ldr/str. Register–memory allows ALU operands in memory.

q: Which model did the 8-bit AVR use?
why: The AVR was load–store too (lds/sts), with one deliberate crack: sbi/cbi on low I/O registers.

q: How many instructions does counter++ on a memory variable take on this chip?
why: The ALU cannot see memory, so it is load, add, store. On x86 it is one instruction.

q: counter++ is 1 instruction on x86 and 3 on Cortex-M. How many bus accesses does each make?
why: Both read the word and write it back: 2 bus accesses. Load–store costs instructions, not memory traffic.

q: What does a load–store design buy in exchange for more instructions?
choices: Fixed-length encoding, a simple decoder and a uniform pipeline
Larger immediate constants packed into every single instruction
why: Fixed 2/4-byte Thumb instructions make a decoder that never asks how long an instruction is, and a pipeline that is the same for every opcode. That is most of what RISC vs CISC meant.

q: How long is a Thumb instruction?
why: Thumb instructions are fixed 2 or 4 bytes. x86 runs from 1 to 15.

q: Why does setting one bit in a peripheral register take three instructions?
choices: The ALU cannot operate on memory: read, modify, write
The register must be unlocked first
Each bit write needs a barrier instruction
The compiler must check the clock gate
why: Load–store means ldr, orrs, str: a read, a modify and a write, with a gap between them that an interrupt can land in.

q: The AVR set a port bit with one sbi instruction. What does the M0+ offer instead?
choices: No single-bit instruction; GPIO's BSRR does it in one str
An sbi instruction that works on any peripheral address below 0x40000000
A bit-band alias region for every register
The bics instruction, which works on memory
why: The M0+ has no sbi. The fix comes back as hardware: BSRR turns a bit-set into a single store (lesson 05). bics works on registers only.

q: A halfword 0xFF9C sits in memory. What do ldrsh and ldrh put in r0?
why: ldrsh copies bit 15 into the upper bits (0xFF9C = −100 stays −100); ldrh fills them with zeros.

q: What does bics r0, r1 compute, and which C produces it?
choices: r0 = r0 AND NOT r1, from x &= ~y
r0 = r0 OR r1, from x |= y
r0 = r0 XOR r1, from x ^= y
why: bics is bit clear: r0 AND NOT r1, the mask-clearing idiom x &= ~y.

q: r0 = 0x000000FF and r1 = 0x0000000F. What is r0 after bics r0, r1?
why: bics clears in r0 every bit that is set in r1: 0xFF AND NOT 0x0F = 0xF0.

q: r0 = 0x5A and r1 = 0xFF. What is r0 after eors r0, r1?
why: XOR with all ones flips every bit: 0101 1010 becomes 1010 0101 = 0xA5.

q: Your M0+ code computes a / b. What instruction does the compiler emit?
choices: A bl to the library routine __aeabi_uidiv
A shift right by b bits
why: The Cortex-M0+ has no divide instruction, so division is a slow library call. sdiv/udiv exist on M3 and above.

q: How can you tell from the .map file that your code divided?
choices: The division helper (_udivsi3) appears in the linked libgcc
The .map file lists the address of every udiv instruction in the image
A warning about division is printed
why: The library routine is only linked in because a line of C divided; its object (libgcc.a(_udivsi3.o)) shows up in Main.map.

q: Why does the M0+ disassembly say adds and movs, not add and mov?
choices: Most 16-bit encodings always set the flags
The s marks a signed operation
The compiler chose to save the flags
why: On the 16-bit Thumb encodings the M0+ uses, there is no room for a choice, so most data-processing instructions always update the flags. On M3+ you pick add or adds.

q: r0 = 0x00010000 and r1 = 0x00010000. What is r0 after muls r0, r1?
why: muls keeps only the low 32 bits of the product. 2^16 × 2^16 = 2^32, whose low 32 bits are all zero.

q: r1 = 5. What does lsls r0, r1, #3 put in r0?
why: A left shift by 3 multiplies by 2³ = 8: 5 × 8 = 40.

q: What value does (2u << (pin * 2)) give for pin = 5?
r1 = 0xFFFFFFF0 (−16 as a signed int). What do asrs r0, r1, #2 and lsrs r0, r1, #2 give?
why: asrs copies the sign bit in from the left, so −16 / 4 = −4. lsrs shifts in zeros, turning a small negative number into a huge positive one.

q: A signed int x is divided by 4 with a logical shift right (lsrs). What goes wrong?
choices: Negative values become very large positive numbers
Positive values are rounded in the wrong direction by the shift
Nothing: lsrs and asrs are identical
why: lsrs is unsigned: it fills with zeros, losing the sign. Signed division needs asrs, which keeps the sign.

q: cmp r3, r2 subtracts and throws the answer away. What is the point?
choices: It sets the N Z C V flags for a later branch
It tests whether r3 is a valid address
It clears r3 if the two are equal
It copies the result into r2
why: cmp is a subtraction that keeps only the flags; the next conditional branch reads them. tst does the same with an AND.

q: How does RISC-V write 'if (a < b) goto L'?
choices: One compare-and-branch instruction: blt a0, a1, L
cmp a0, a1 followed by blt L
A subtract, then a branch on the N flag
It has to call a library routine
why: RISC-V and MIPS are compare-and-branch machines with no flags register: the comparison and the branch are one instruction.

q: Which flag indicates signed overflow?
why: N negative, Z zero, C carry/borrow, V signed overflow.

q: blt and bcc both mean 'less than'. What is the difference?
choices: blt is signed, bcc is unsigned
blt is unsigned, bcc is signed
blt compares registers, bcc compares constants
why: blt/bge are signed comparisons; bcc/bcs are unsigned (lower / higher-or-same). The compiler picks by the variable's signedness.

q: r0 = 0xFFFFFFFF, r1 = 1. After cmp r0, r1, which branches are taken?
choices: blt is taken; bcc is not
bcc is taken; blt is not
why: Signed, 0xFFFFFFFF is −1 < 1, so blt is taken. Unsigned, it is 4 294 967 295, not lower than 1, so bcc is not.

q: Where does a signedness bug (blt where bcc was needed) usually show up?
choices: Only at the extremes of the value range
why: Signed and unsigned agree for small positive values; they disagree only near the top of the range, so the bug hides until extreme values appear.

q: r0 = 5 and r1 = 5. Which flag does cmp r0, r1 set that makes beq take the branch?
why: 5 − 5 = 0, so the zero flag Z is set and beq (equal) is taken.

q: What does bl func do?
choices: Jumps to func and saves the return address in LR
Jumps to func and pushes the return address
Jumps to func only if the last compare was lower
Loads func's address into a register
why: bl is branch with link: the return address goes into LR, not onto the stack.

q: What does pop {r4, pc} do that pop {r4, lr} does not?
choices: It returns: popping into PC is a branch
It restores the flags as well
It frees the stack frame of the caller
why: Loading PC is a branch, so popping the saved LR straight into PC is the return, saving a bx lr.

q: Which machines put a call's return address on the stack?
why: Stack-based: x86, 68000, AVR (rcall/ret). Link register: ARM, RISC-V (ra), MIPS (ra), PowerPC.

q: Why does a non-leaf function start with push {…, lr}?
choices: LR holds only one return address, and its own bl would overwrite it
AAPCS requires every function, leaf or not, to save LR on the stack
The hardware needs LR on the stack to return
why: A call it makes will put a new return address in LR, so the old one must be saved first. A leaf function can skip it.

q: Which addressing mode does s->field compile to?
choices: Register offset, like ldrb r6, [r1, r3]
why: A struct field is base plus a constant offset known at compile time. That is also how USART2->ISR is reached.

q: Which addressing mode does buf[i] compile to?
choices: Register offset, like ldrb r6, [r1, r3]
why: An array index is base plus a variable offset computed at run time: register offset.

q: Can the M0+ compile *p++ into a single post-indexed ldr r0, [r1], #4?
choices: No: pre/post-indexed and scaled forms are M3+ only
Yes: all Thumb cores have post-indexed loads in 16 bits
Yes, but only for byte loads
Only if p points into SRAM
why: Scaled register, pre-indexed and post-indexed modes are 32-bit encodings on M3 and above. The M0+ needs a separate adds.

q: What range of offsets can a 16-bit ldr r0, [r1, #n] encode?
why: 5 bits scaled by 4 give 0–124. ±4095 is the M3/M4 32-bit form; 0–1020 is the SP-relative form.

q: A 16-bit ldr has its 5-bit offset field set to 9. What byte offset is that?
why: The field is stored divided by 4, so 9 means 36. (The slides' 7 means 28, 10 means 40.)

q: Which offset can a single 16-bit ldr r0, [r1, #n] encode?
why: It must be a multiple of 4 between 0 and 124. 126 is not a multiple of 4, 128 is out of reach and negative offsets do not exist in 16-bit Thumb.

q: A driver reads a register at offset 0x90 from its peripheral's base. What happens on the M0+?
choices: The compiler adds to the base first, costing an extra instruction
The access faults, because the offset cannot be reached from the base
It is one 16-bit ldr like any other
The linker places the register closer to the base
why: 0x90 = 144 is beyond 124, so the compiler emits an add to move the base and then loads. Large peripheral structs get worse code at the far end.

q: FLASH->ACR = (FLASH->ACR & ~LATENCY) | LATENCY_0; compiles to which four instructions?
why: Load the register, bics for the & ~, orrs for the |, store back: one statement, read-modify-write.

q: FLASH->ACR reads 0x00000602. What is written back by ACR = (ACR & ~0x7) | 0x1?
why: Clear bits 2:0: 0x602 → 0x600. OR in 1: 0x601. Bits outside the field are untouched.

q: Which word would a literal pool hold for the mask ~(3 << 4)?
why: 3 << 4 = 0x30; inverting every bit gives 0xFFFFFFCF, all ones except bits 5:4. The slides' ~(7 << 11) is 0xFFFFC7FF the same way.

q: A literal pool contains the word 0x00B71B00. Which constant from C is it?
why: 0x00B71B00 = 12 000 000, the 12 MHz reset clock. (0x02DC6C00 is 48 000 000, four times as large.)

q: Why does the compiler load 0x40021000 with ldr r2, [pc, #44] instead of movs?
choices: A 32-bit constant cannot fit inside a 16-bit instruction
PC-relative loads are faster than movs
Peripheral addresses must always be read from flash, never built in a register
why: The constant is parked in a literal pool after the function and loaded PC-relative. movs only holds an 8-bit immediate.

q: How does RISC-V get a 32-bit constant into a register?
choices: Builds it in two halves with lui then addi
Loads it from a literal pool, PC-relative
Embeds it in a longer instruction
why: RISC-V uses lui + addi; AArch64 movz/movk; x86 makes the instruction longer; ARM/Thumb uses a literal pool. movw/movt is the M3/M4 Thumb-2 way.

q: Is the literal pool an ARM-specific quirk?
choices: No: every fixed-width ISA needs some way to build 32-bit constants
Yes: no other architecture ever needs to keep its constants in memory
Yes: it exists only because of the Thumb bit
No: it is needed only for floating-point values
why: A 16- or 32-bit instruction cannot carry an arbitrary 32-bit constant, so every fixed-width machine needs an answer. ARM's is the literal pool.

q: Which constant can a single 16-bit movs r0, #n load on the M0+?
why: movs has an 8-bit immediate, 0–255. 300 and the address need more bits; −1 is not in 0–255.

q: A polling loop on a status register compiles to which pattern?
why: ldr the register, ands/tst to isolate the bit, cmp, bne back to the ldr. It costs the CPU every cycle until the hardware agrees.

q: Without volatile on the status register, what would the optimiser do to a polling loop?
choices: Read the register once and loop forever on the cached value
Delete the whole loop, since reading a value has no side effects
why: Without volatile the compiler may read once into a register and test that copy forever, so the loop hangs.

q: A 16-bit bne at 0x08000300 has offset imm8 = 0xFC (−4 halfwords), counted from PC + 4. Where does it branch?
The constant 0x80 and the USART2 base appear before the loop though the C uses them inside it. Name the transformation.
why: Anything that cannot change is lifted out of the loop: hoisting.

q: uart2_putc is a function in the source but _write contains no bl. Why?
choices: The compiler inlined it at each call
It was hoisted out of the loop
It was removed as dead code
The linker replaced it with printf
why: Inlining: its three instructions appear once for '\r' and again for the character.

q: Why does a debugger stepping through -Os code seem to jump around?
choices: Address order is not source order after reordering
The debugger loses the Thumb bit
Breakpoints only work on even addresses
Each source line compiles to exactly one instruction, so steps are uneven
why: The compiler rotates and reorders blocks; return len sits in the middle of _write's address range.

q: In _write, buf[i] is loaded twice, before and after the store to USART2->TDR. Why?
choices: A char object may alias anything, so the store might have changed it
The volatile qualifier on buf forces every load from it to happen twice
The compiler ran out of registers
The UART needs the byte read twice
why: Character types may alias any object, so the compiler cannot assume the store left buf[i] unchanged.

q: USART2 is at 0x40004400 and its ISR is at offset 28. What address does ldr r6, [r4, #28] read?
why: 28 = 0x1C, so 0x40004400 + 0x1C = 0x4000441C. 0x28 is decimal 40, the TDR offset.

q: The USART TXE flag is bit 7. Which constant tests it?
why: 1 << 7 = 128 = 0x80; _write loads it with movs r0, #128.

q: What is the Cortex-M0+'s instruction set?
why: The M0/M0+ is ARMv6-M, Thumb-1 plus six. M3 is ARMv7-M full Thumb-2; M4/M7 add DSP.

q: Which of these is one of the M0+'s only 32-bit instructions?
why: The six are bl, mrs, msr, dsb, dmb, isb. udiv, movw and wide ldr belong to Thumb-2 on M3 and above.

q: How does the M0+ do conditional execution?
choices: With IT blocks of up to 4 instructions
With a condition on every instruction
why: IT blocks are M3+; ARM (A32) conditions every instruction. The M0+ only has conditional branches.

q: Why do most 16-bit Thumb instructions reach only R0–R7?
choices: R8–R12 are reserved for the OS
R8–R12 only exist in ARM state
why: Three bits name eight registers. The 32-bit forms on M3+ reach all 16.

q: A Thumb-2 decoder reads a halfword whose top five bits are 11101, 11110 or 11111 as the start of a 32-bit instruction. Which halfword starts one?
why: 0xF000 begins 11110. 0xD1FB begins 11010, 0x4A0B 01001 and 0x6811 01101: all 16-bit instructions.

q: Why is bl a 32-bit instruction on the M0+?
choices: A call must reach anywhere; a 16-bit branch reaches only about ±2 KB
All calls must store a full 32-bit return address in LR, which needs 32 bits
why: Thumb widens only when 16 bits cannot do the job at all, and a call must reach the whole address space.

q: Which of these cores has a hardware floating-point unit?
why: Only M4F and M7 have an FPU. The M3 has hardware divide but no FPU; the M0+ has neither.

q: The adds everywhere, no divide, 0–124 offsets, R0–R7 only: what are these limits of?
choices: The Thumb instruction set in general
why: None of those are ARM; they are Thumb-1. The same C on a Cortex-M4 (Thumb-2) gets add, sdiv and ldr r0, [r1, #2000].

q: Which can a Cortex-M4 do in ONE instruction that the M0+ cannot?
choices: bl to a function 1 MB away
why: Thumb-2's 32-bit loads reach ±4095. The M0+ can do the other three (bl is one of its six 32-bit instructions).

q: Under AAPCS, where are a function's first four arguments and its result?
choices: Arguments in r0–r3, result in r0
Arguments in r4–r7, result in r4
Arguments on the stack, result in r0
Arguments in r0–r3, result in r3
why: r0–r3 carry arguments 1–4 and the result comes back in r0. They are caller-saved scratch.

q: A function uses r5 for its loop counter. Who must make sure r5 is unchanged afterwards?
choices: The function itself: r4–r11 are callee-saved
why: r4–r11 are callee-saved: a function that uses them pushes and restores them, like _write's push {r4–r7, lr}.

q: A function you call may destroy which registers without restoring them?
why: r0–r3 and r12 are caller-saved scratch; the caller saves anything in them it still needs.

q: Why does a calling convention such as AAPCS exist?
choices: Code compiled separately must agree on who owns which register
It lets the CPU check argument types at run time
It makes interrupts save fewer registers
It is required for the Thumb bit to work
why: Your C calls libraries built years ago by other compilers or written in assembly; the ABI is the agreement that makes that work.

q: A handler starts at 0x080001A0. What value goes in its vector-table slot?
why: Every code address handed to the core has bit 0 = 1, the Thumb bit: 0x080001A0 | 1.

q: The reset vector holds 0x08000275 but Reset_Handler is at 0x08000274. What happens if you 'fix' it to 0x08000274?
choices: The chip faults at reset: bit 0 clear means ARM code
It works: the core ignores bit 0
Execution starts one byte late and skips the first instruction
The core switches to ARM state and runs
why: Bit 0 = 1 means Thumb. Clear it and the core is told to run ARM code it does not have, so it faults immediately.

q: A 4-byte bl sits at 0x08000300. What value is in LR inside the called function?
why: The return address is the next instruction, 0x08000304, and bl sets bit 0: LR = 0x08000305.

q: LR reads 0x0800028F. Where does bx lr continue?
why: bx lr branches to LR & ~1, the instruction right after the call. Nothing is skipped and nothing is off by one.

q: A HardFault's stacked PC or LR is a sensible even address. What does that usually mean?
choices: A computed function pointer or a mov pc, lr return lost the Thumb bit
The fault happened inside an interrupt handler, which always uses even addresses
why: An even code address is a branch into ARM state. Typical causes: a function pointer computed rather than assigned, or hand-written assembly returning with mov pc, lr instead of bx lr.

q: Inside an exception handler, LR reads 0xFFFFFFF9. What is it?
choices: An EXC_RETURN value; branching to it unstacks the frame
A corrupted return address left behind by a stack overflow in the handler
The address of the vector table
An odd return address with the Thumb bit set
why: In a handler LR holds a magic EXC_RETURN value (0xFFFFFFF9 or 0xFFFFFFFD), not a return address.

q: What is the compiler obliged to preserve when it optimises?
choices: Only the program's observable behaviour as C defines it
The exact order of every source line
Every memory access in the source
The register each variable is assigned to, as declared in the source
why: The as-if rule: only C-defined observable behaviour. It may hoist, inline, reorder and cache in registers, and C has never heard of your peripheral.

q: Code works at -O0 and hangs at -Os. Classic cause?
choices: A missing volatile on something hardware changes
why: At -Os the compiler caches the value in a register and never rereads it. volatile forbids that.

q: How do CMSIS headers protect peripheral registers from the optimiser?
choices: Every register is declared __IO, which is volatile
They wrap each access in a function call
They disable compiler optimisation for every file that includes peripheral code
They put registers in a non-cached section
why: CMSIS declares every register __IO = volatile, so you inherit the protection.
